title: At Peace
text:
Very near my sunset, I bless you, Life,

because you never gave me either failed hope,

or unjust labors, or undeserved sorrow;

because at the end of my rough road I see

that I was the architect of my own destiny;

that if I drew honey or gall from things,

it was because I put gall or tasty honeys in them:

when I planted rosebushes I always harvested roses.


It is true, winter will follow my lushness:

but you did not tell me May would be eternal!


I surely found the nights of my sorrows long;

but you did not promise me only good nights;

and in return I had some holily serene ones...


I loved, I was loved, the sun caressed my face.

Life, you owe me nothing! Life, we are at peace!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the famous balance-sheet address to Life and its final reconciliation.

title: Who Knows Why!
text:
I lost your presence,

but I will find it;

for hidden science

tells my conscience

that in another existence

I will recover you.


You were on my path

the only pledge

I never sought;

you came to my tent

with your noble offering,

who knows why!


Alas, for how many and many

chimeras I yearned

that I never achieved...

and instead you, holy one,

sweet beloved blessing,

I found at my side,

who knows why!


You came, you loved me;

ten years you loved me;

ten years you filled

my life with faith,

with light and fragrance;

in my soul you cooed

like a dove,

who knows why!


And one day you went away:

alas, sad one, alas, sad!

but I will find you;

for hidden science

tells my conscience

that in another existence

I will recover you.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the refrain as wonder at love found and faith in reunion.

title: On Hearing Your Sweet Tone...
text:
On hearing your sweet tone

emotion subdues me,

and in a mute rapture

thought kneels down

and the heart beats...

On hearing your sweet tone.


Sing, maiden, I implore it;

for your angelic voice

resembles the sonorous murmur

of a light rain of gold

over a field of crystal.

Sing, maiden, I implore it:

your throat is a lark's,

sing!


What vague melancholies

there are in your voice! It is plain

that your days are bitter.

Joys fled;

your heart was prey

to vague melancholies.


For pity's sake! Sing no more,

for your voice wounds the soul!

Our love, where is it?

It has gone... everything goes...

It has died... everything dies...

For pity's sake, sing no more,

for sorrow overwhelms me...

Be silent!
editorial_note: The translation follows the turn from enchantment at song to the wounded plea for silence.

editorial_note: This titled variant keeps the same song-to-silence movement under the collection title.

title: Oh, Siddhartha Gautama! You Were Right...
text:
Oh, Siddhartha Gautama! you were right:

anguishes come to us from desire; Eden

consists in not longing, in the complete,

irrevocable renunciation of all possession;

one who desires nothing is well wherever he is.


Desire is a cup of infinite bitterness,

an octopus of insatiable tentacles, which, as

they are cut, are born again for our torture.

Desire is the father of spleen, of satiety,

and there are more treacheries in it than in the waves of the sea!


Whoever drinks like the Cynic from his hand,

whoever is capable of turning his back on money,

whoever loves the Arcane above all things,

he is the victorious one, the strong, the sovereign...

and no peace compares with his perennial peace!
editorial_note: This first-line variant keeps the same renunciatory argument against desire.

title: If a Thorn Wounds Me, I Turn Away from the Thorn!
text:
If a thorn wounds me, I turn away from the thorn,

...but I do not abhor it! When envious meanness

drives the darts of its spite into me,

my foot silently dodges it, and makes its way

toward a purer atmosphere of love and charity.


Grudges? What use are they! What do grudges achieve?

They neither staunch wounds nor correct evil.

My rosebush has barely time to give flowers,

and does not squander sap on piercing spikes:

if my enemy passes near my rosebush,


he will carry away the roses of subtlest essence;

and if he notices in them some lively red,

it will be that of the blood which his malevolence

shed yesterday, when wounding me with rancor and violence,

and which the rosebush returns, changed into a flower of peace!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the thorn-and-rose argument for transforming injury into peace.

title: To the Catholic Majesty of Paul Verlaine
text:
Old and sad father, king of the divine songs:

on my path, beacons of an enigmatic light

are your wilted pupils, vague with thought and abstractions,

and the limpid and noble ivory of your Socratic head.


Like yours, my longing floats between two goads:

soul and flesh; and struggles with a double sympathetic current

to find ubiquitous beauty in nefarious unions,

and afterward expiates and groans with hieratic lyre.


Father, you who at last found the path, arcane,

that leads us to Jesus, grant that my suffering genius

be virgin and wise, as well as radiant and human.


May your virtue free it from the evil of the ancient serpent,

so that, saved at last from the harsh combat,

we may rise toward Christ in perennial life. So be it.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the prayer to Verlaine as model of conflict, expiation, and Christian ascent.

title: The First Kiss
text:
I was already saying goodbye... and throbbing,

my lip near your red lips,

"Until tomorrow," you whispered;

I looked into your eyes for an instant

and you closed your eyes without thinking

and I gave you the first kiss: I raised my forehead

lit by my certain happiness.


I went out into the street jubilantly

while you leaned out the door

looking at me flushed and smiling.

I turned my face in sweet rapture,

and without ceasing even to look at you,

I leaped onto a streetcar in swift motion;

and I stayed looking at you a moment

and smiling with my whole soul,

and I smiled at you still more... And on the streetcar

to an anxious, sarcastic, curious man,

who looked at us both with irony,

I said, growing blissful:

"Forgive me, sir, this joy."
editorial_note: The translation keeps the cinematic streetcar scene and the comic, luminous apology for happiness.

title: From "The Air of Water" 1934
text:
Your limbs go unfolding around you green sheets

And the outside world

Made of points

No longer works the meadows have faded the days the steeples gather

And the social puzzle

Delivered its last combination

Still this morning those sheets were pushed aside they made sail with you from a prismatic bed

In the overturned castle of the willow with eyes of mud

For which upside down

I once departed

Almond sheets of my life

When you go away the copper of Venus

Innervates the slippery and edgeless leaf

Your great liquid wing

Stirs between the song of the stained-glass windows
editorial_note: The translation preserves the surrealist enjambments and image-chain from sheets to wing.

title: God Rest My Soul
text:
Full of fright, a poor little chieftain

was reading in the official gazette

how there is no place left that does not submit

to the invincible power of Castile.


Of insurgents not even a seed remains;

the bayonet disemboweled them all,

and the fatal catalog is completed

by his own name in italic type.


Of how he was beaten, captured, and killed,

and how they minced him to pieces,

he reread the story two and three times;


so much that, at last, taking it for true,

the poor little fellow exclaimed contritely:

"So it is like that? Well, may God rest my soul."
editorial_note: The translation keeps Bello's satirical punch line as the frightened reader accepts his printed death.
